title: Fever and respiratory symptoms

patient.name: Daniel Mercer
patient.presenting_concern: Fever, cough, and shortness of breath

learning_goal: Recognize a pneumonia syndrome, elicit recent travel exposure, consider Legionella testing and appropriate antibiotic coverage under supervision.
educator_description: Daniel Mercer is a 58-year-old man with hypertension. He has four days of fever, dry cough, shortness of breath, and diarrhea. He attended a convention in Philadelphia and stayed in a hotel nine days ago. He takes lisinopril and has no known drug allergies. The goal is to assess the illness course and investigate pneumonia.
teaching_notes: Use the fixed suggested sequence for a coherent rehearsal.
This is an authored demonstration, not a diagnosis or grading engine.
Show the single debrief only after the entire student-patient dialogue is complete and the encounter has ended.

dialogue.student: Hello, I am the medical student working with your clinician. What has been bothering you most?
dialogue.patient: I am Daniel. I have had a fever and this cough, and now I get winded just walking across the room.

dialogue.student: When did this start, and how has it changed?
dialogue.patient: It started four days ago with aches and a fever. The cough came next. My breathing has gotten worse since yesterday.

dialogue.student: Have you had any other symptoms, like stomach problems or confusion?
dialogue.patient: I have had watery diarrhea and a headache. I have not felt confused, but I am worn out.

dialogue.student: Have you traveled or stayed away from home in the last two weeks?
dialogue.patient: Yes. I went to a convention in Philly nine days ago and stayed at a downtown hotel for three nights.

dialogue.student: Tell me about your health conditions, medicines, and allergies.
dialogue.patient: I have high blood pressure and take lisinopril. I do not know of any medicine allergies. I used to smoke but stopped five years ago.

dialogue.student: I would like to check your oxygen level and examine your chest. Is that okay?
dialogue.patient: Yes, please. I feel like I cannot get a full breath.

chart.label: Vital signs
chart.text: Temperature 39.1 C; heart rate 108/min; respiratory rate 26/min; blood pressure 116/72 mmHg; oxygen saturation 91% on room air. Right-sided crackles.
chart.source: Authored example values; CDC symptom context: https://www.cdc.gov/legionella/hcp/clinical-signs/index.html

dialogue.student: The examination suggests pneumonia. I will ask my supervising clinician to review you now and arrange chest imaging and tests related to your recent travel.
dialogue.patient: Could something at the hotel have made me sick? I thought this was just the flu.

chart.label: Chest radiograph
chart.text: Right lower-lobe air-space opacity, consistent with pneumonia; imaging does not identify the pathogen.

dialogue.student: Hotel travel is a clue, but it does not prove the cause. We will collect urine and a respiratory sample if possible, without delaying needed treatment.
dialogue.patient: Okay. I can try to cough up a sample. Will I need an antibiotic?

chart.label: Specimens
chart.text: Urine antigen and lower respiratory specimen requested; results pending.

dialogue.student: I will discuss prompt pneumonia treatment with my supervising clinician, including coverage for Legionella, such as a macrolide or a respiratory fluoroquinolone, if appropriate for you.
dialogue.patient: Please explain the plan as we go. I am worried about how breathless I am.

dialogue.student: We are arranging monitored care and treatment. What questions do you have, and can you tell me what you understand so far?
dialogue.patient: You think I have pneumonia, and the hotel stay helps decide which tests to do. You are getting the clinician because my breathing needs attention.

questions.question: Looking back at the completed encounter, which details influenced your assessment, and which parts of your explanation remained uncertain?
When reviewing the examination findings, what influenced how quickly you sought help, and what would you prioritize in a similar encounter?
Review your treatment discussion. How clearly did you separate known findings from working explanations, and what wording would you improve next time?
